title: The Arcanum's Syllabus
summary: The founding articles of the Arcanum.

claims.text: The Syllabus sets out a search for knowledge for its own sake, aimed at the members' enlightenment and in the end all humanity's.
It holds that another world, where ancient myth is true, touches this one, and that only scholarship can tell real lore from superstition.
Members are to observe, not judge or act on the supernatural by any fixed code, and the society's findings are not shared with outsiders.

title: Founding of the Arcanum
summary: How Benjamen Holmscroft gathered nine scholars into a society in the 1880s.

claims.text: Nine founders from Britain, Ireland, Boston and Rome formed the first Arcanum, with Holmscroft Manor as the root of a hoped-for network of houses.
The founders sat as the Executive Committee and chose Holmscroft as Grand Chancellor, with near total power.
Holmscroft wrote the society's rituals, first held at Christmas 1885; a founder suspected they were far older than the Arcanum.

title: Arcanum houses, colonies and lodges
summary: How the Arcanum organises its members.

claims.text: Colonies are houses in training: groups with no funds of their own that report to the nearest full house until the area proves busy enough to earn full status.
Field research on hauntings and the like is done in groups, for witnesses and safety; members who work together regularly form a lodge, often from one class of Neophytes.
The Foundation House stands in the Fens of Cambridgeshire, and a London house in a Georgian townhouse handles business and outside meetings.
The society first grew across Europe, from Berlin, Vienna, Paris and Prague to Amsterdam, Madrid and Stockholm; the Dublin House draws students of fae lore.

title: Arcanum factions
summary: The informal camps that divide the Arcanum.

claims.text: Seekers treat the work as a personal quest for the Grail or the Stone and dismiss whatever they do not count as sacred.
Progressivists want to strip away the Victorian trappings and secrecy and remake the society as a modern institution.
The Executive Committee now and then orders a lodge to drop a case as trivial or wasteful, which feeds suspicion that secrets are buried inside the society.
